   Haze in Singapore: PM2.5 readings ‘normal’ in northern, southern, eastern regions

 and Clay Lim
 Published   Oct 21, 2026, 06:09 AM

 Set as preferred source Listen Summarise Singapore’s air quality improved on Oct 21, with all regions at “normal” PM2.5 levels at 1pm and the north, south and east still normal at 4pm.
 The west and central regions remained in the “elevated” PM2.5 band, while the 24-hour PSI was “unhealthy” in the west and central, showing haze still affected parts of the island.
 NEA warned unhealthy air could continue on Oct 21 as haze from Kalimantan drifts in. Free N95 masks are being given to vulnerable groups, and more masks are on sale.
 AI generated
 SINGAPORE – The air quality in Singapore generally improved on Oct 21, as compared with the day before, with all regions registering “normal” PM2.5 levels at 1pm.
 As at 7 pm, the day’s PM2.5 readings across five regions here ranged from 14 to 92 , while readings for Oct 20 ranged from 19 to 111.
 PM2.5 readings for the north ( 34 ), south ( 51 ) and east ( 49 ) were in the “normal” band as at 7pm, while the west ( 92 ) and central ( 61 ) are in the “elevated” zone.
 Earlier at 1pm, all regions registered “normal” PM 2.5 levels. This was the first time that current air quality across Singapore was in the normal range since the period between noon and 2pm on Oct 19, and before that, on Oct 4.
 The one-hour PM2.5 readings are measured in micrograms per cubic metre and are a gauge of the current air quality.
 Scores from zero to 55 represent normal values, those between 56 and 150 indicate an elevated concentration of fine particles, while readings between 151 and 250 are considered high and scores above 251 are classified as very high.
 PM2.5 – fine particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter – is the dominant pollutant during periods of transboundary haze, and small enough that they can bypass the nose and throat and penetrate deep into the lungs and bloodstream.
 For healthy people, short-term exposure to high levels of haze particles may cause irritation of the eyes, nose, and throat. Haze particles can affect the heart and lungs, especially in people who already have chronic heart or lung disease, such as asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or heart failure.
 The highest PM2.5 reading this haze season was recorded at 3pm on Oct 14 in the western part of the island at 288.
 Meanwhile, the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) continued to hover between the good to moderate and unhealthy bands.
 At 7pm, the readings were in the “unhealthy range” at 123 in the west and 108 in the central, while readings for the rest of Singapore were in the “ good to moderate” range: north ( 80 ), south ( 87 ) and east ( 92 ).
 The 24-hour PSI readings were in the unhealthy band in four out of the five regions – south, east, west and central – for most of the evening on Oct 20.
 Air quality is considered “good to moderate” when the PSI – a 24-hour rolling average of six key air pollutants – is in the range of 0 to 100, and “unhealthy” when it is in the range of 101 to 200. Beyond 200, it enters the “very unhealthy” band.
 The highest 24-hour PSI reading this haze season was recorded at 10am on Oct 18, when it hit 230 in the western region, in the very unhealthy range.
 Unhealthy air quality forecast for Oct 22
 In an advisory on the evening of Oct 21 , the National Environment Agency (NEA) said that unhealthy air quality is expected on Oct 22 . PSI levels may range from 101 to 160 .
 Showers fell mainly over western Singapore this afternoon and smoke haze from Kalimantan was observed near Singapore, the agency said.
 Smoke haze was also observed over Sumatra.
 While showers are forecast over Singapore and the surrounding region on Oct 22, dry conditions are expected over the southern parts of Kalimantan, NEA said.
 Under prevailing east-southeasterly or southeasterly winds, smoke haze from fires in Kalimantan may be transported towards Singapore, it added. 
 Smoke haze from fires in the region may continue to drift towards Singapore on Oct 23 due to southeasterly or south-southeasterly winds.
 On Oct 24, winds are expected to shift to blow towards the south-west. Given the dry conditions forecast over southern and central Sumatra, smoke haze from Sumatra may drift towards Singapore, NEA added.
 Singapore is currently experiencing its 17th day of unhealthy air – surpassing the 14-day stretch during the 2015 haze crisis, during which bad air persisted from Sept 23 to Oct 7.
 The authorities have begun distributing free N95 masks to vulnerable people, such as the elderly, expectant mothers, younger children and people with medical conditions such as asthma.
 N95 masks form a tight seal around the face, and can filter out 95% of fine particles between 0.1 and 0.3 micrometres in size.
 The Ministry of Health on Oct 20 said that N95 or equivalent masks – including KN95, KF94 and FFP2 models – can be bought at all FairPrice outlets, as well as pharmacies such as Guardian, Unity and Watsons.
 They will also be made available for purchase progressively at all Cold Storage, Giant and Sheng Siong outlets by the end of the week.
